name: Sesame
summary: A warm-season annual grown for edible seeds and oil, with flowers that attract pollinators. UF/IFAS gives home-garden planting guidance; variety, shattering behavior, and mature size vary, so no benne cultivar or harvest trait is assumed.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Sesamum indicum L. UF/IFAS describes sesame as a home-garden seed crop and distinguishes heirloom benne from modern sesame types. This record is species-level and does not claim a particular seed color, cultivar, or shattering trait.

growth.short: Warm-season annual with upright stems and tubular flowers
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS describes an upright annual with showy bell-shaped flowers and reports typical plant sizes varying with cultivar and conditions. NC State's production profile gives an even wider field range. No single mature dimension is assigned to an unspecified seed source.

cultivation.short: Warm soil, full sun and drainage; avoid waterlogged conditions
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends planting after soil exceeds 68°F and full sun, and describes poor performance in overly moist soils in Florida. NC State's field production guidance likewise warns against waterlogging. These regional soil recommendations do not establish hydroponic suitability.

care.short: Watch capsules as they mature because some types shatter
care.guidance: UF/IFAS notes that mature capsules can burst and spill seed, while shatter-resistant cultivars exist. Harvest timing and capsule behavior depend on cultivar; this identity does not assume non-shattering genetics.

harvestUse.short: Edible seeds used whole or for oil
harvestUse.guidance: UF/IFAS describes sesame seed use as a condiment, in pastes and for oil. It also describes harvesting dry stalks carefully to limit capsule shattering; no universal harvest date is assigned.

problems.short: Waterlogging and capsule shattering are important risks
problems.guidance: NC State reports poor tolerance of saturated soil; UF/IFAS describes capsule shattering at maturity. These are crop management risks and vary with site and variety.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field and soil home-garden evidence does not validate hydroponic sesame production.

evidence.note: UF/IFAS describes an upright growth habit.

height.reason: Sources report broad cultivar- and environment-dependent ranges; no seed source or cultivar is specified.

spacing.reason: Field-row spacing does not establish container or pod capacity.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun is not normalized into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Purple Pitcher Plant
summary: A North American carnivorous bog perennial with upward-facing pitchers. NC State Extension documents high-sun, persistently wet, acidic, low-nutrient conditions and cold-stratified seed; never collect wild plants because the species is protected in the wild.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Sarracenia purpurea L. and recognizes two subspecies. NC State uses purple pitcher plant and northern pitcher plant. This entry does not assign a subspecies, cultivar, or source population.

growth.short: Carnivorous perennial with rosette pitchers and rhizome offsets
growth.guidance: NC State describes pitchers that recline near the ground with openings upward and rhizome offsets that form small colonies. Its dimensions are regional species ranges and are not a container-system capacity claim.

cultivation.short: Full sun and continuously wet, acidic, low-nutrient medium
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends moist-to-wet acidic conditions, says containers must not dry out, and advises rain or distilled water because the plant is sensitive to minerals and household-water chemicals. It says not to fertilize or feed the plant. This is bog/container horticulture, not evidence for nutrient-solution hydroponics.

propagation.short: Rhizome division and seed are documented routes
propagation.guidance: NC State lists division and seed propagation and notes that seeds germinate after cold stratification; it does not give the stratification duration here. Purchase plants from reputable carnivorous-plant nurseries and do not collect wild specimens, as the source notes wild protection.

problems.short: Mineral-rich tap water, drying and fertilizer can harm this bog-adapted plant
problems.guidance: NC State warns about sensitivity to minerals and chemicals in household water, drying, and fertilizer/feeding. Monitor for listed pests and root rot; the source does not claim a disease-free species.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Bog container culture and mineral-sensitive water requirements do not establish a suitable hydroponic system.

evidence.note: NC State describes rosette pitchers and rhizome offsets forming colonies.

height.reason: Regional species range is not a standardized indoor/cultivar height.

spread.reason: A bog colony's landscape spread is not a single-container footprint.

spacing.reason: Bog-garden spacing is not Garden pod capacity.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun does not establish an indoor light tier.
